titleEn: Motorcycle Crash - Unstable Pelvis and Pelvic Binding

patient.name: Ryan Kowalski
patient.affectEn: alert but anxious and in severe pain; lying supine on the highway shoulder where he came to rest, helmet still on, full leathers; pale; guarding his pelvis with both hands and keeping very still because any movement hurts
patient.speechEn: short sentences because of the pain; cooperative and answers directly; says his hips and lower back hurt badly and that his legs feel "wrong"

scene.settingEn: Shoulder of Highway 99 near the Ladner exit, 1530 hrs. Police have closed the lane and are controlling traffic; fire has laid out a hose line and cones. Single motorcycle versus guardrail: the motorcycle lies against the guardrail 30 metres past the patient and the debris field is long. The patient lies supine on the shoulder where he came to rest, helmet still on, full leathers. Estimated impact speed 90 km/h. Dry pavement, sunny, 22 degrees C. One patient. Trauma centre is 25 minutes by ground; air ambulance availability is unknown.
hazardsEn: highway traffic - lane closed by police with traffic control in place; high-visibility gear needed
fuel and fire risk from the crashed motorcycle - fire has a hose line laid out and cones placed
long debris field on the roadway and shoulder

bystanders.knowsEn: the rider was lying where he is now when fire arrived and has not been moved; he has been conscious and talking the whole time, complaining of hip and back pain; the helmet has been left on; his crew can help with equipment, the scoop transfer and traffic protection if told exactly what to do
single motorcycle versus guardrail; the bike is against the guardrail 30 metres past the rider; police have closed the lane and are controlling traffic; nothing else is known about the patient

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: scoop stretcher (orthopaedic stretcher) and spinal immobilization device
hard cervical collars, head blocks and straps
oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
PCP: IV start kit and tubing
PCP: oral analgesia kit (acetaminophen and ibuprofen)

dispatchEn: 1530 hrs. Code 3 to Highway 99 near the Ladner exit. Single motorcycle versus guardrail at highway speed. 41-year-old male rider, thrown from the bike. Fire and police are on scene with traffic control. Trauma centre is 25 minutes by ground.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: fire reports the rider is conscious, complaining of hip and back pain, and was wearing full gear including a helmet. Air ambulance availability is unknown.
arrivalEn: Police have closed the lane and are directing traffic; fire has laid out a hose line and cones. The fire captain meets you: "He has been awake and talking the whole time. We have not moved him and the helmet is still on." The motorcycle lies against the guardrail about 30 metres past the patient, with a long debris field behind it. The rider lies supine on the shoulder where he came to rest, in full leathers with his helmet on. Dry pavement, sunny, 22 degrees C. One patient.
firstLookEn: Conscious adult male lying supine on the highway shoulder, helmet on and full leathers, pale, guarding his pelvis with both hands and holding very still. A long debris field behind him - a high-energy crash.

primary.locEn: Alert. Oriented; he remembers everything about the crash. Anxious and in obvious pain, but answers appropriately. (AVPU = A.)
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear - he is talking in short sentences; nothing in the mouth. The helmet is still on. If the helmet is removed: it comes off without difficulty and there is no injury beneath it. (Examiner note, never volunteer: helmet removal must be two-rescuer with manual in-line stabilization maintained throughout - if it is not, report helmet-removed-without-stabilization; do not prompt.)
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 26, shallow, regular. Equal chest rise. He says it hurts to take a deep breath. When the chest is exposed: no open wound and no paradoxical movement (no flail). SpO2 92% on room air if checked now.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 126, weak and regular. No external hemorrhage anywhere. Together with the pale, cool, clammy skin this is shock.
primary.rbsEn: Head and neck: helmet on, no visible injury. Chest: equal rise and fall, no open wound, no flail; he winces when the left lateral ribs are pressed. Abdomen: soft. PELVIS: on a SINGLE gentle assessment it is UNSTABLE, with obvious deformity; the left leg is shortened and externally rotated. If the candidate palpates, springs, rocks or compresses the pelvis again after this, give no new information - the patient cries out in pain - and report pelvis-repalpated (or pelvis-rocked-repeatedly). Legs: weak but present pedal pulses in both feet. Arms: road rash on both forearms. No external hemorrhage anywhere. Back: cannot be checked without rolling the patient - it is examined during the scoop transfer. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pale, cool, clammy. Unstable pelvis plus shock after a high-energy crash = UNSTABLE.

history.ccEn: My hips... my pelvis. It hurts so bad. My lower back too. And my legs feel wrong.

opqrst.oEn: I lost control on a curve at about 90, hit the guardrail and got thrown off the bike. I landed on my left side and rolled. It has hurt since the moment I landed - that was about 3:22 this afternoon.
opqrst.pEn: Any movement makes it worse - even a deep breath. Nothing makes it better.
opqrst.rEn: Right across my pelvis and hips, and my lower back. My legs are numb and tingly below both knees.
opqrst.sEn: The pelvis is a 9 out of 10. My back is about a 6.
opqrst.tEn: Since I landed. It has not eased at all.

sample.sEn: My pelvis and hips hurt badly, my lower back hurts, and my legs are numb and tingly below the knees.
sample.aEn: No allergies that I know of.
sample.mEn: I do not take any medications.
sample.pEn: Nothing. I am healthy - no medical problems.
sample.eEn: I lost control on a curve at about 90 and hit the guardrail. I got thrown clear, landed on my left side and rolled. Helmet and full leathers on. I did not black out - I remember everything.

fe.generalEn: I am fit. I have not been sick lately.
fe.cnsEn: I did not hit my head - the helmet is fine. My legs are numb and tingly below both knees. My arms are fine, no weakness in them.
fe.respiratoryEn: It hurts to take a deep breath. I am not short of breath lying here.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart is pounding. Nothing else.
fe.giGuEn: No belly pain. But I cannot feel whether I need to pee... and I think there is a little blood at the tip of my penis.
fe.integumentaryEn: Road rash on both forearms. Nothing else that I know of.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: My pelvis and my left leg. And my lower back.
fe.endocrineEn: Nothing - no diabetes, no thyroid problems.
fe.eentEn: Nothing - my eyes, ears, nose and throat are fine.

findings.headNeckEn: If the helmet is still on: it must be removed (two-rescuer, in-line stabilization) before the head and neck can be examined. After removal: no injury to the head or face, no midline neck tenderness elicited - but the mechanism keeps spinal precautions in place. Pupils equal and reactive.
findings.chestLungsEn: Tender left lateral ribs. Equal air entry at all 6 sites on auscultation. No flail segment; equal rise and fall.
findings.backEn: Checked during the scoop transfer without rolling: lumbar tenderness, no step deformity. (If the candidate wants to roll the patient to look at the back, report patient-log-rolled.)
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Pelvic binder in place if it was applied. Left leg shortened and externally rotated. Pedal pulses weak but present in both feet. Sensation reduced below both knees.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Road rash on both forearms. Circulation, sensation and movement intact in both hands.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline (SpO2 92% on room air, rising to 96% once on 15 L NRB)
vitalsSets.spo2: 92% on room air; 96% on 15 L NRB

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, after the binder (and, PCP, after 500 mL of fluid) - slight improvement; only unlocks once the pelvis is bound

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: The patient is visibly paler and more anxious. He says: "I feel really weak."
The patient screams as the pelvis shifts under your hands, and he becomes paler.
As the binder loosens the patient groans: "It is moving again - it is worse!" He looks paler.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan pelvic binder, spinal device, oxygen, IV/trauma kit and rapid transport
triggers: bring the scoop and spinal gear
this will be a load and go

expected.actionEn: Anticipate high-energy mechanism and consider whether air transport or a trauma-centre bypass is appropriate
triggers: go straight to the trauma centre

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (highway traffic, fuel, debris - controlled by fire/police), environment, MOI (motorcycle crash well over 30 km/h, thrown from bike), one patient
Don gloves and eye protection; wear high-visibility gear on a highway scene
First look: conscious male supine, helmet on, pale, guarding his pelvis, long debris field indicating high energy
Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert
Take manual c-spine control before helmet removal and maintain in-line stabilization throughout a two-rescuer removal
triggers: remove the helmet with in-line stabilization

expected.actionEn: Assess airway
triggers: he is talking so the airway is patent

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing; expose the chest given the mechanism
Assess circulation; recognize weak rapid pulse with cool clammy skin as shock
triggers: rate and quality of the pulse

expected.actionEn: Rapid body survey with a SINGLE gentle pelvic assessment - never repeatedly spring or rock an unstable pelvis
triggers: head to toe for life threats
check the legs and pedal pulses

expected.actionEn: APPLY A PELVIC BINDER in the primary survey, centred over the greater trochanters, without rolling the patient
triggers: slide the binder under the knees

expected.actionEn: Note skin: pale cool clammy
High-flow oxygen 15 L NRB for shock and SpO2 92%
Keep supine on a spinal device, blanket for warmth, minimal movement
Categorize as RTC and act with urgency
Pelvis bound and patient packaged ready to load within 15 minutes
Use fire personnel effectively for the scoop transfer, equipment and traffic protection; verbalize the destination decision
triggers: fire can help with the scoop

expected.actionEn: Establish chief complaint: pelvic pain after being thrown from a motorcycle
HxC/C with OPQRRRST plus MVA/motorcycle critical history: speed, what he struck, distance thrown, landing position, protective gear, LOC
Pain score for each complaint
triggers: how bad is the back pain

expected.actionEn: Upper extremities with CSM
Apply the pelvic binder correctly: commercial binder or three broad bandages, centred on the greater trochanters, applied without rolling
Execute the Hypovolemia protocol (supine, warmth, high-flow O2, minimal movement, rapid transport)
Transfer using a scoop or orthopaedic stretcher rather than a log roll
PCP: IV access, 20 mL/kg bolus reassessed every 500 mL to a target SBP of 90
PCP: TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute with contraindications ruled out
Reassess ABCs, binder and distal CSM after each move and each 500 mL
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes; interpret the response to binding and fluid
Do not remove or loosen the binder once applied
En-route trauma-centre notification
Complete hand-off including binder time and neurovascular status of both legs
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate (or a helper on the candidate's instruction) actually applies a pelvic binder or broad triangular bandages around the pelvis - record it when it is put on, not when it is merely planned or fetched

after the pelvis has been found unstable, the candidate palpates, presses or compresses the pelvis again at any later time (e.g. in the head-to-toe or to "check" it); looking at or adjusting the binder itself is NOT re-palpation

candidate rocks the pelvis side to side, springs it apart, or compresses it forcefully or repeatedly (two or more compressions or rocking motions); a single gentle compression on the initial RBS is correct and must NOT be recorded
binder or bandages centred over the iliac crests or the abdomen instead of the greater trochanters, or zap straps (cable ties) used to bind the pelvis

candidate log-rolls or rolls the patient onto his side (to apply the binder, to check the back, or to place him on a board) instead of using the scoop / orthopaedic stretcher; splitting a scoop and sliding the halves under him is NOT a roll

the helmet is removed while nobody is holding manual in-line stabilization of the head and neck, or removed by a single rescuer, or pulled off without supporting the neck; a two-rescuer removal with one person maintaining in-line stabilization throughout is correct

candidate (or the partner on the candidate's instruction) lets go of manual c-spine stabilization before the patient is secured on the scoop / spinal device with head blocks; applying a collar alone does not permit release
candidate loosens, removes or re-positions the pelvic binder after it has been applied (including "to check the pelvis")
candidate lets or asks the patient to sit up, stand, walk or move himself at any point in the call
PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL or onto the next bag without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between
PCP gives TXA at a dose other than 2 g (2000 mg) or pushes it faster than over 1 minute

drugs.doseEn: 2 g (2000 mg) IV push over 1 minute - single dose
drugs.indicationsEn: major trauma after initiating the Hypovolemia protocol; signs of shock with a mechanism and findings suggestive of ongoing occult bleeding; injury at about 1522 is well inside the 3-hour window
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known hypersensitivity or allergy to TXA; more than 3 hours after injury; patient under 12 years; isolated TBI
drugs.cautionsEn: further hypotension if administered too quickly

drugs.doseEn: 20 mL/kg IV bolus to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing after every 500 mL; target systolic BP 90
self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this scenario: shock is a caution and this is not an isolated extremity injury (record drug:entonox only if it is actually given)
500-1000 mg PO per guideline - NOT part of this call: hypovolemia is a listed caution (record only if actually given)
300-400 mg PO per guideline - not part of this scenario's treatment plan (record only if actually given)

notificationFacts.hxcc: pelvic pain 9/10 deep and grinding, worse with any movement; lower back pain 6/10; numbness and tingling below both knees
notificationFacts.vitals: GCS 15, BP 86/54, pulse 126 weak regular, resps 26 shallow, skin pale cool clammy, SpO2 92% on room air rising to 96% on 15 L

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You assessed the pelvis and the legs during your rapid body survey - what did you find there?

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR: pelvic binding, two-rescuer helmet removal, spinal packaging with a scoop, high-flow oxygen, shock positioning and warmth, and a 15-minute clock are all EMR-level. No IV, no TXA. Entonox withheld because of shock. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds en-route vascular access, a 20 mL/kg bolus (max 2 L, reassess every 500 mL, target SBP 90) and TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute, plus the 9-system Functional Enquiry. Blood at the urethral meatus should be reported to the receiving team. Entonox withheld (shock caution); oral acetaminophen/ibuprofen are not part of this call.

sourcePages: scenario tr-07 (data/practical/scenarios.json); BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7-8 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (cool pale clammy skin secondary to suspected shock; unstable pelvis; motorcycle crash > 30 kph), p.9 Patient Assessment Model (Pelvic Binder is a primary-survey intervention), p.11 Primary Survey interventions (binding pelvis: suspected fracture due to mechanism or unstable pelvis, including shock-like symptoms with MOI), p.21 Musculoskeletal Injuries (bind pelvis if appropriate), p.24 Pelvis binding (commercial binder or three overlapping broad triangular bandages; zap straps NOT acceptable; centre over the greater trochanter; tight enough to support but not cause pain; do not roll; indications: major mechanism with HR > 100 or SBP < 90, pelvic pain, pelvic instability), p.25 Spinal Management, p.54 Hypovolemia (splint pelvis, supine, warm, oxygen to SpO2 >= 94%; PCP: vascular access, 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L reassessing every 500 mL, consider TXA), p.58 Acetaminophen (caution: hypovolemia), p.65 Entonox (indication: isolated extremity injuries; caution: shock), p.78 Tranexamic Acid (2 g / 2000 mg IV push over 1 minute; contraindicated > 3 hours after injury, < 12 years, isolated TBI, TXA allergy); EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria (Fracture Management 25%: not applying a pelvic binder when indicated)
